localAi.whatNeverHolds: If the model is slow or down, mail is never held up.

outcome.pendingHint: The server stopped before it finished.

audit.exportBody: The records the filters above match, up to 100,000, newest first. Each line carries its chain hash, and the file ends with a manifest, so whoever receives it can check it. The export itself is recorded.
audit.reasonHint: Ticket, request or case this is for
audit.verifiedBody: Every record on every node follows from the one before it. This catches edits to the store; it can’t stop someone with root on the server rewriting everything, so forward records to a system your mail administrators don’t control as well.
audit.brokenBody: At least one record doesn’t follow from the one before it. Keep the server as it is and compare against an export or a forwarded copy.
audit.retentionBody: Older records are removed once a day. At least 90 days; the default is two years. This change is recorded too.

certCard.guidedHint: Pick domains, check every name first, and watch Let’s Encrypt certificates arrive. About two minutes.
certCard.manualHint: Add an ACME provider, then set each domain’s Certificate management yourself.
certCard.title: Free certificates that renew themselves
certCard.hint: A guide checks your domains’ names and sets up Let’s Encrypt, so certificates are issued and renewed for you.

certSetup.title: Certificates, automatically
certSetup.subtitle: Free certificates from Let’s Encrypt for your domains, renewed by the server before they expire.
certSetup.howTitle: How the server proves it’s yours
certSetup.howDns: A domain whose DNS is connected is checked through DNS: the certificate covers the domain and everything under it (*.domain), and nothing needs to reach this server.
certSetup.howTls: Otherwise Let’s Encrypt connects to this server on port 443 for each name. Those names must point straight at this server, not through a proxy.
certSetup.checkedHow: Each name is looked up in public DNS through {{resolver}}, and compared with where {{server}} points. Nothing is ordered yet.
certSetup.whyAllText: One certificate covers all of a domain’s names. If a single name fails, the whole order fails and keeps retrying.
certSetup.dnsReady: {{domain}}: checked through its connected DNS, covering {{names}}.
certSetup.noAnchor: This server’s own address couldn’t be looked up, so names are only checked for existing.
certSetup.missing: doesn’t exist: add a CNAME to {{server}}
certSetup.proxied: goes through the Cloudflare proxy: set it to DNS only (grey cloud)
certSetup.fixOr: Fix those names in DNS and check again, or
certSetup.connectDnsWhy: so it’s checked through DNS instead.
certSetup.anyway: Order anyway (it will keep retrying until the names are fixed)
certSetup.stagingText: Let’s Encrypt’s staging service issues certificates that browsers don’t trust, with far looser limits. Use it to see everything work, then run this guide again without it.
certSetup.contactHint: Let’s Encrypt writes here only about problems with your account or certificates. Creating the account accepts their Subscriber Agreement.
certSetup.reuse: The Let’s Encrypt account already set up on this server will be used.
certSetup.stagingHint: Certificates browsers won’t trust. For trying this out.
certSetup.undo: Set a domain’s Certificate management back to Manual. Certificates already issued stay until they expire.
certSetup.newAccount: A Let’s Encrypt {{kind}}account is added for {{email}}.
certSetup.skipped: Left as they are until their names are fixed: {{names}}.
certSetup.coveredAlready: Already covered by a certificate valid until {{date}}; it renews on {{due}}.
certSetup.after: The server renews each certificate well before it expires. Failed renewals show under Management › Tasks › Failed.
certSetup.watchingHint: Checking every few seconds. Most certificates arrive within a minute.

dirCard.guidedHint: Pick your directory, fill in the connection, test a person, then choose domains. Nothing moves until the test passes.
dirCard.manualHint: Create the directory and set each domain’s directory yourself.
dirCard.title: Sign in with accounts you already have
dirCard.hint: A guide connects Active Directory, LDAP or an OpenID Connect provider, tests a real person, then moves the domains you pick.

dirSetup.notLoaded: The server hasn’t loaded the directory yet.
dirSetup.title: Connect a sign-in directory
dirSetup.subtitle: Let people sign in with the accounts they already have in Active Directory, LDAP or an OpenID Connect provider.
dirSetup.safe: The directory is saved and tested on its own first. Sign-in only moves to it for the domains you pick at the end.
dirSetup.sql: An SQL database as a directory is set up by hand, under Directories.
dirSetup.bind: A read-only account the server uses to find people. Each person’s own password is then checked by signing in as them.
dirSetup.oidc: Register inbuxa as a client there. Mail apps can’t do browser sign-in, so people use app passwords for IMAP and SMTP.
dirSetup.urlHint: ldaps:// on 636 is encrypted from the start. ldap:// uses STARTTLS unless it’s this machine.
dirSetup.keep: Leave empty to keep the saved one
dirSetup.invalidCertsHint: Only for a self-signed test server. Anyone in between could read passwords.
dirSetup.usernameDomainHint: Added to a user name without @, to make the address.
dirSetup.testHow: The server looks the address up in the directory and, if you give a password, signs in as that person. Nothing is created here, and a wrong password doesn’t count against anyone.
dirSetup.opened: The server can use this directory.
dirSetup.foundGroup: That address is a group, not a person. Try a person’s address.
dirSetup.notFound: Nobody with that address. Check the search base and that the address is in the mail attribute.
dirSetup.wrongPassword: The directory says that password is wrong.
dirSetup.fixHint: Go back to change the connection. Saving again updates the same directory.
dirSetup.who: On a domain that moves to this directory, only people the directory knows can sign in with a password. Existing accounts it doesn’t know stop signing in and, for LDAP, stop receiving mail. App passwords keep working.
dirSetup.yours: You sign in on this domain.
dirSetup.asDefaultHint: For every domain without a directory of its own. Rarely what you want: prefer choosing domains.
dirSetup.lockout: This includes the account you’re signed in with ({{me}}).
dirSetup.lockoutHint: If the directory doesn’t know you, you can’t sign in again with your password. Test your own address first, keep an app password, or leave that domain out.
dirSetup.understood: I’ve checked I can still sign in
dirSetup.undo: Set a domain’s directory back to the server default. Accounts made from the directory stay, with the last password it supplied.
dirSetup.countNote: ; its {{count}} existing accounts must be in the directory
dirSetup.defaultMoves: Every other domain without its own directory signs in through {{dir}}.
dirSetup.doneHint: Have someone sign in to the webmail with their directory password. Their account is created on first sign-in, with the name, aliases and groups the directory gives.

rules.wordsHint: One word or phrase per line
rules.disclaimerHtml: HTML version (optional; the text is used otherwise)
rules.warnBody: The sender sees the notice and may send anyway, giving a reason that’s recorded.
rules.holdBody: It waits under Held mail until a reviewer releases or rejects it.
rules.blockBody: It isn’t sent, and the sender sees the notice.
rules.name: Name
rules.conditions: When all of these are true
rules.exceptions: Except when any of these is true
rules.stop: Stop here: later rules don’t run for this message
rules.unavailable: This server doesn’t have mail rules.
rules.dlpSubtitle: Rules that check outgoing mail for what shouldn’t leave (card numbers, national ID numbers, keys, your own words) and warn, hold it for review, or block it. Every match is in the audit log, never what was found.
rules.flowSubtitle: Rules that change mail as it passes: disclaimers, banners, headers, copies, redirects, refusals. They run after the server’s own Sieve script, in the order below.
rules.noneDlp: No DLP rules yet: outgoing mail isn’t checked.

dnsWizard.createFailed: The provider could not be saved.
dnsWizard.updateFailed: The domain could not be switched to automatic DNS.
dnsWizard.title: Publish DNS for {{domain}}
dnsWizard.subtitle: Connect your DNS host once, and the server keeps these records right for you.
dnsWizard.whatBody: Your mail server writes its own DNS records through your DNS host’s API: mail routing, the records that prove your mail is yours, and the ones mail apps use to set themselves up.
dnsWizard.whatKeep: When keys rotate or settings change, it updates them again. Nothing is changed until the last step.
dnsWizard.detecting: Looking up where {{domain}}’s DNS is hosted…
dnsWizard.byHand: Add the records by hand instead
dnsWizard.unsupportedHint: The server can’t update that host for you, but adding the records by hand takes a few minutes, and this page checks each one as it goes live.
dnsWizard.notFoundHint: Once it’s registered and pointed at a DNS host, you can add the records by hand or connect the host here.
dnsWizard.notRight: Not right? Choose your DNS host
dnsWizard.chooseHost: Using a host the server can update? Choose it
dnsWizard.keepNarrowBody: Give the server a credential that can edit DNS for this domain and nothing else. If it ever leaked, that’s all it could touch.
dnsWizard.storedBody: It’s stored in the server’s settings and never shown again. You can replace or remove it on the DNS provider’s page.
dnsWizard.unsupported: This provider needs settings the guided setup can’t take. Add it on the DNS providers page, then come back and choose it here.
dnsWizard.recordsNoteBody: Only the names listed here are written. Records the server doesn’t own, like your website or other TXT entries, are left as they are.
dnsWizard.originHint: Only if {{domain}} lives inside a bigger zone at your host, for example mail.example.com kept in example.com.
dnsWizard.happensRest: {{domain}} switches to automatic DNS, and the server starts writing records straight away. Most hosts show them within a minute or two.
dnsWizard.undoBody: If anything fails here, nothing is kept. Later, switching the domain back to manual stops all updates, and the records already written stay where they are.
dnsWizard.alreadyAuto: This domain already publishes automatically; this updates its settings.
dnsWizard.howCheckedBody: Every few seconds this page asks {{resolver}} for each record, so a green tick means the whole internet can see it.
dnsWizard.undoLive: Switch the domain’s DNS management back to manual to stop updates. Records already written stay.
dnsWizard.taskFailedShort: Your DNS host turned the update down.
dnsWizard.taskPending: The server is writing the records to your DNS host…
dnsWizard.keepsUpdating: From now on the server keeps them up to date by itself.
dnsWizard.waiting: Written. Waiting for them to show up in public DNS, which can take a few minutes.
dnsWizard.failedRecords_one: {{count}} record wasn’t written. Your DNS host said:
dnsWizard.failedRecords_other: {{count}} records weren’t written. Your DNS host said:
dnsWizard.failedHelp: Check that the credential can edit this zone, then fix it on the DNS provider’s page. The server retries on its own.
dnsWizard.differentHelp: An amber mark means that name has a different value right now, often an old record that hasn’t expired from caches yet.

dnsCopy.subtitle: Add these at your DNS host. Each one ticks green as the internet sees it.
dnsCopy.how1: In your DNS host’s panel, add a record for each row: pick the type, paste the name and the value.
dnsCopy.how2: The name is shown the way most panels want it: “@” means {{zone}} itself. If yours asks for full names, add .{{zone}} to the end.
dnsCopy.how3: Set the TTL to Auto or one hour. If a record with the same name and type exists, replace it.
dnsCopy.zoneHint: For hosts that can import a zone file
dnsCopy.copyZone: Copy all as a zone file

dnsCard.title: Let the server publish your DNS records
dnsCard.autoHint: See which records are live, or change what it publishes.
dnsCard.hint: Connect your DNS host, such as Cloudflare, and skip copying records by hand. Optional.
dnsCard.guidedHint: Pick your DNS host, paste a key, choose records, and watch them go live. About two minutes.
dnsCard.manualHint: Use the DNS Management setting below, with every option at once.

eventPicker.search: Search events, e.g. bounce, ban, certificate

webhookTest.title: Send a test event
webhookTest.body: One sample event of type webhook.test, sent with the saved settings, even while the webhook is off. Save changes first to test them.

webhooks.title: What a webhook receives
webhooks.body: A POST with a JSON body holding one or more of the events you chose, batched at most once per throttle interval:
webhooks.signature: With a signature key set, each request carries X-Signature: the HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body under that key, in base64. Compute it on your side and compare before trusting the request.
webhooks.try: To see one arrive, choose “Failed sign-ins and bans” and sign in once with a wrong password. Failed deliveries are retried until “Discard after”.

legacyProtocols.bannerTail: on this server. Only inbuxa webmail and JMAP apps can sign in.
legacyProtocols.bannerTailTenant: for your organization. Only inbuxa webmail and JMAP apps can sign in.
legacyProtocols.unavailable: This server does not offer the legacy protocols switch.
legacyProtocols.title: Legacy mail protocols
legacyProtocols.subtitle: Turn off IMAP, POP3 or ManageSieve one at a time, or all of them with sending from mail apps, so that only inbuxa webmail and JMAP apps can reach this server.
legacyProtocols.strandedTitle: Some listeners could not be reopened
legacyProtocols.strandedBody: Their ports may be taken by something else, or need a restart to bind. They are kept, and can be tried again:
legacyProtocols.statusOff: Legacy mail protocols are off on this server.
legacyProtocols.statusOffBody: Only inbuxa webmail and JMAP apps can sign in.
legacyProtocols.statusSomeBody: Mail apps can still use {{list}}, and send.
legacyProtocols.statusOnBody: Mail apps can use IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve.
legacyProtocols.rowSubmission: On; sign-in refused only with all three off
legacyProtocols.lockNote: Incoming mail (SMTP) and inbuxa webmail (JMAP) are locked open: closing them would stop mail arriving and lock everyone out, including you.
legacyProtocols.submissionNote: Sending from mail apps goes on while any of IMAP, POP3 or ManageSieve is on.
legacyProtocols.tenantOff: Off for {{organization}}. Only inbuxa webmail and JMAP apps can sign in to its domains.
legacyProtocols.tenantSome: Some are off for {{organization}}. Mail apps can still send, and use what is on.
legacyProtocols.tenantOn: On for {{organization}}. Mail apps can use IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve on its domains.
legacyProtocols.oneLead: Mail apps using {{protocol}} will stop working for {{scope}}. The other protocols, sending from mail apps, and inbuxa webmail are not affected.
legacyProtocols.oneNobody: No account used {{protocol}} in the last 30 days.
legacyProtocols.oneUsers_one: 1 account used {{protocol}} in the last 30 days:
legacyProtocols.oneUsers_other: {{count}} accounts used {{protocol}} in the last 30 days:
legacyProtocols.onePorts: Its ports close: {{ports}}. Your firewall and port forwarding are not changed.
legacyProtocols.oneNoPorts: No {{protocol}} listener is configured, so no port closes.
legacyProtocols.oneUndo: You can turn it back on at any time.
legacyProtocols.impactNone: No account used a legacy mail app in the last 30 days.
legacyProtocols.impactCount_one: 1 account used a legacy mail app in the last 30 days.
legacyProtocols.impactCount_other: {{count}} accounts used a legacy mail app in the last 30 days.
legacyProtocols.impactLeadAll: Their mail apps stop working when what they use is turned off:
legacyProtocols.statementTitle: Only inbuxa webmail and JMAP apps will work.
legacyProtocols.statementLead: Legacy mail protocols (IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve and sending from mail apps) will be turned off for everyone on this server.
legacyProtocols.statementLeadTenant: Legacy mail protocols (IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve and sending from mail apps) will be turned off for everyone in {{organization}}.
legacyProtocols.statementApps: Phone and desktop mail apps will stop receiving and sending mail. That’s iPhone and iPad Mail, the Gmail and Outlook apps, Outlook, Thunderbird and Apple Mail. People will see sign-in errors in them.
legacyProtocols.statementFilters: Filters managed from a mail app (ManageSieve) will stop working. Filters set in inbuxa webmail keep working.
legacyProtocols.statementUnaffected: Incoming mail is not affected. Calendars and contacts are not affected.
legacyProtocols.statementWebmail: People keep full access through inbuxa webmail, which can be installed as an app on phones and computers.
legacyProtocols.statementPorts: The IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve ports will close: {{list}}.
legacyProtocols.statementNoPorts: No IMAP, POP3 or ManageSieve listeners are configured, so no ports will close.
legacyProtocols.statementSubmission: Sending from mail apps (SMTP submission) will stop working, but its ports stay open: mail apps will be told they cannot sign in. Incoming mail (SMTP) and inbuxa webmail (JMAP) are not affected and cannot be turned off here.
legacyProtocols.firewallLead: This does not change your firewall or port forwarding.
legacyProtocols.firewallBody: inbuxa stops answering on these ports; anything that still routes them to this server — firewall rules, NAT port-forwards, a load balancer or proxy — is yours to reconcile.
legacyProtocols.statementUndo: You can turn legacy protocols back on at any time.

logRetention.title: Log files
logRetention.forever: Rotated log files are kept with no limit. They record client IP addresses and email addresses.
logRetention.days_one: Rotated log files are deleted after 1 day, on every server.
logRetention.days_other: Rotated log files are deleted after {{count}} days, on every server.

hold.heldTitle: Held: nothing in this account can be destroyed, and deleting it keeps its data.
hold.scopeHint: Domains, groups and tenants count as they are now: an account added later is held, and one that leaves stays held.
hold.reasonHint: Why, for the audit log: counsel’s letter, a matter number…
hold.placed: Hold placed. What it covers can no longer be destroyed.
hold.editBody: A hold can grow, never shrink: more accounts, or a wider date range. To hold less, release it and place a new one.
hold.placeBody: Nothing it covers can be destroyed: deletions are kept in the archive with no expiry, by any user, delegate or administrator, and deleted accounts keep their data. People aren’t told.
hold.name: Case name
hold.rangeHint: Leave both empty to hold everything. With dates, mail counts by when it arrived and events by when they start; contacts, files and filter scripts are held whole. Without an end, mail still to come is held too.
hold.releaseFailed: The hold is still in place
hold.releaseBody: What only this hold kept gets its normal deadline back, and never less than 30 days from now, so a mistaken release can be undone by placing a new hold. Anything another hold covers stays held. A released hold stays listed, and can’t be put back.
hold.typeName: Type the case name to confirm: {{name}}

export.title: Export {{name}}
export.body: Collects everything this hold covers into one ZIP: mail as .eml, calendars as .ics, contacts as .vcf, files as they are, and the deleted items it keeps, with a manifest of SHA-256 checksums. It runs on the server; you can leave this page.
export.accounts: People (leave empty for everyone the hold covers)
export.accountsHint: Someone the hold doesn’t cover is left out of the file.
export.reasonHint: Why, for the audit log: a production request, a matter number…
export.heading: Exports
export.expiry: Only the person who started an export can download it. The file is kept as a temporary upload (an hour, unless the upload time-to-live says otherwise); the record, with its checksum, stays.

hold.since: From {{from}}, and mail still to come
hold.unavailable: This server can’t place legal holds.
hold.title: Legal holds
hold.subtitle: Nothing a hold covers can be destroyed, by anyone, until it is released: deletions are kept with no expiry and deleted accounts keep their data. People aren’t told.

limitsSetup.title: Sending and receiving limits
limitsSetup.subtitle: Sensible rate limits for the people who use this server. Without any, one stolen password can send as much spam as it likes.
limitsSetup.personalHint: A handful of people you know. Low limits: nobody here sends in bulk.
limitsSetup.organizationHint: Tens to hundreds of known people, some of whom send a lot in a day.
limitsSetup.hostingHint: People you don’t know sign up. Tight sending limits, because compromised accounts are the risk.
limitsSetup.handSome: The {{count}} rules made by hand are left exactly as they are.
limitsSetup.handNone: Rules you add by hand later are never touched by this guide.
limitsSetup.over: Incoming: the other side is told to try again later. Outgoing: the delivery waits in the queue and goes out when the rate allows. Nothing is lost.
limitsSetup.undo: Run the guide again, or switch any rule off in its list. Rules the guide wrote start with “Preset:”.
limitsSetup.nothing: These limits are already in place. Nothing changes.
limitsSetup.doneHint: Each list shows its rules in plain words:

limitsSummary.guidedHint: Say who uses this server and get five sensible limits, each shown as a sentence you can adjust.
limitsSummary.manualHint: Add and edit each rule yourself, with every option.
limitsSummary.none: No limits here yet: nothing is slowed down or refused.
limitsSummary.title: In plain words

lock.bannerTitle: Locked: receives mail, can’t sign in, sends nothing on its own.
lock.title: Locked accounts
lock.subtitle: Accounts that keep receiving mail but can’t sign in and send nothing on their own, for someone who left, an investigation or a compromised account. Delegates can open them beside their own mail.

access.readHint: Sees everything, changes nothing. Reading doesn’t even mark mail read.
access.organizeHint: Also flags, files and moves mail and makes folders. Never deletes.
access.fullHint: Everything the owner could do, deleting included.

lock.reasonHint: Why, for the audit log: a ticket, a case, “left the company”…
lock.delegatesHint: People who can open this account, beside their own mail, while it is locked. Everything they do there is recorded.
lock.sendAs: May send as this account (its Sent keeps a copy)
lock.locked: Account locked. Its open sessions were ended.
lock.lockBody: Mail keeps arriving, but nobody can sign in to the account, by any means, and it sends nothing on its own: no forwarding, no vacation reply, no read receipts. Open sessions end now.
lock.unlockBody: The account can sign in again and its forwarding and vacation reply resume. Delegates lose it, and any shares they had before get back what they were. The password is unchanged: if someone else may know it, set a new one on the account’s page too.

metricsConnect.needsLogin: It answers, and asks for the user name and password: as it should.
metricsConnect.cantCheck: The browser couldn’t read it (usually cross-site rules). Check the target on your Prometheus instead.
metricsConnect.title: Where the server’s numbers go
metricsConnect.promHint: Prometheus fetches them from this server every so often.
metricsConnect.open: Without a user name anyone who can reach the server can read these numbers, which show how busy it is.
metricsConnect.shownOnce: The new password is in the scrape job below. It’s shown only now: copy it before you leave.
metricsConnect.otel: Send them to an OpenTelemetry service
metricsConnect.keep: Leave empty to keep the saved one
metricsConnect.hcKeyHint: An ingest key from your Honeycomb environment’s API keys.
metricsConnect.gcEndpointHint: From your stack’s OpenTelemetry page in the Grafana Cloud portal.
metricsConnect.gcTokenHint: An access policy token with metrics:write. Needed again whenever these settings change.
metricsConnect.delta: This server sends counters as deltas. If some counters don’t show up, put an OpenTelemetry Collector with the deltatocumulative processor in between.
metricsConnect.collectorHttpHint: /v1/metrics is added if it isn’t there.
metricsConnect.pushEvery: The server sends them once a minute.
metricsConnect.more: Which metrics, and every setting on this page

ports.https: Webmail, this console, JMAP apps, automatic setup
ports.http: Redirect to HTTPS, and HTTP certificate checks
ports.title: The standard ports
ports.reach: Open here means the server listens. Whether the internet can reach it also depends on your firewall and hosting provider.

reachability.title: Reachable from outside
reachability.clusterBody: Each server tries the others’ ports every {{minutes}} minutes, over the internet, by their public names.
reachability.localBody: A single server can’t see its own firewall from inside, so this only says whether each port is listening here. To check from outside, try from another network: nc -vz <this server’s name> <port>.

reports.more: Names, subjects and every setting on this page
reports.byRule: by a rule on its page
reports.title: Reports, in short
reports.dmarcSentence: Tell other domains how mail claiming to be from them fared here (DMARC)
reports.tlsSentence: Tell them whether their mail reached us encrypted (TLS)
reports.failureSentence: Report each message that fails their checks (DMARC, DKIM, SPF), at most once a day per address
reports.mixed: Set differently on the DMARC, DKIM and SPF pages. Switching here sets all three.
reports.privacy: These include the failing message’s headers, which carry people’s addresses. Most large providers don’t send them.
reports.fromSentence: Send them, and bounce messages, from addresses at
reports.inboundAfter: and show them under Management › Reports
reports.inboundHint: Separate addresses with commas. * matches any domain: postmaster@* is every domain’s postmaster.
reports.forwardSentence: Then deliver them to that mailbox as well

retention.more: Schedules and every setting on this page
retention.title: How long things are kept
retention.holds: Mail under a legal hold is kept whatever these say: deleting it archives it, and it doesn’t expire while held.

senderLevels.relaxedHint: Checks everything and hands the results to the spam filter, but refuses nothing. The server’s stock setting.
senderLevels.recommendedHint: Also refuses mail forged in the name of a domain that asks for that (DMARC p=reject), and checks forwarding chains (ARC).
senderLevels.strictHint: Also refuses senders without matching reverse DNS or a passing SPF record. Expect to lose some real mail from small or badly set-up servers.
senderLevels.iprev: Reverse DNS of the sending server
senderLevels.dmarcReject: Refused if the domain says reject
senderLevels.failed: The level could not be saved.
senderLevels.title: How strict to be with incoming mail
senderLevels.footnote: Checks run on port 25, where other servers deliver; mail from your own signed-in users isn’t checked. No level refuses unsigned mail: most legitimate mail would bounce.
senderLevels.replaces: This replaces the six checks below, including any conditions you added to them. DKIM signing isn’t touched.

sendingCard.guidedHint: Check port 25, choose direct delivery or a relay service, and see exactly what changes. About three minutes.
sendingCard.manualHint: Edit the delivery strategy and routes yourself, with every option.
sendingCard.title: Direct delivery or a relay?
sendingCard.hint: A guide checks whether port 25 is open and sets up Amazon SES, Mailgun, SendGrid or another relay for you.

sendingSetup.title: How this server sends mail
sendingSetup.subtitle: Deliver straight to other mail servers, or hand outgoing mail to a relay service that delivers it for you.
sendingSetup.whyDirect: Direct delivery needs port 25 open to the internet, an IP address with a clean reputation, and reverse DNS that names this server.
sendingSetup.whyRelay: A relay suits a home connection or a cloud host that blocks port 25, or when you’d rather someone else handle reputation. It costs a little and the service sees your outgoing mail.
sendingSetup.undo: Run this guide again and pick the other way. A relay you set up stays saved, unused, so switching back is quick.
sendingSetup.nowDirect: Right now this server delivers directly.
sendingSetup.nowRelay: Right now outgoing mail goes through a relay: {{host}}.
sendingSetup.nowOther: Right now outgoing mail follows a custom rule ({{target}}). Choosing here replaces that fallback.
sendingSetup.checkHint: Connects from this server to a big mail provider’s servers on port 25 and waits for their greeting. Nothing is sent.
sendingSetup.checkOpen: Port 25 is open: {{host}} answered. Direct delivery can work.
sendingSetup.checkBlocked: Port 25 looks blocked ({{reason}}). Your host probably filters it: use a relay, or ask them to open it.
sendingSetup.directHint: This server looks up each recipient’s mail servers and delivers to them itself. No third party, nothing to pay.
sendingSetup.relayHint: Amazon SES, Mailgun, SendGrid, Postmark, Brevo, SMTP2GO or your ISP’s server. It delivers for you and handles reputation.
sendingSetup.otherHint: Your ISP’s or provider’s outgoing server.
sendingSetup.regionHint: The region your account sends from.
sendingSetup.stored: The password is saved in this server’s settings, like other secrets, and is never shown again here.
sendingSetup.keepPassword: Leave empty to keep the saved one
sendingSetup.rollback: The changes are written one at a time. If one is refused, the ones before it are put back, so a failed attempt leaves things as they were.
sendingSetup.nothing: This server already sends mail this way. Nothing needs to change.
sendingSetup.keptHint: Your {{count}} other routing rules still apply first, before this fallback.
sendingSetup.where: Settings › Mail flow › Sending holds the delivery strategy and routes this guide changed, for anything it doesn’t cover.
sendingSetup.doneDirect: This server delivers outgoing mail directly.
sendingSetup.test1: From the webmail, send a message to an address outside your domains, such as a personal Gmail or Outlook account.
sendingSetup.test2b: . A delivery lists each attempt and the answer from the other side.
sendingSetup.test3Relay: , its last error says why: usually the sign-in, or a sender domain the relay hasn’t verified yet.
sendingSetup.test3Direct: , its last error says why: often port 25 being blocked, or the other side rejecting this server’s IP.

settingsOverview.title: Settings
settingsOverview.subtitle: The menu above groups everything the server does by job. Anything you change is marked against its default.

spamLevels.relaxedHint: Only clear spam goes to Junk. Some spam reaches the inbox; almost nothing real is misfiled.
spamLevels.balancedHint: The server’s stock setting. Likely spam goes to Junk; nothing is refused.
spamLevels.strictHint: More goes to Junk, and blatant spam is refused outright. The sender of a misjudged message gets a bounce.
spamLevels.title: How hard the spam filter is
spamLevels.discardWarning: A discard threshold is set by hand. Picking a level turns it off: deleted mail can’t be found again, and nobody is told.
spamLevels.trustReplies: Never treat replies to people’s own messages as spam
spamLevels.trustContacts: Never treat mail from people in their address book as spam
spamLevels.pyzor: Check messages against Pyzor’s shared spam list
spamLevels.pyzorHint: Sends a fingerprint of each message, not the message itself, to public.pyzor.org.
